text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers on Tuesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Sweden mourns Prince Bertil who died at his home in Stockholm on Sunday aged 84. Thousands go to the Royal Palace in Stockholm to sign the official condolence list. His funeral will be held on January 13 at the palace's chapel.

- Every fourth person aged over 70 who lives alone does not think anyone would notice if they fell sick. Ten percent of elderly people living alone did not know who to turn to if they were ill, according to a survey by a social services committee.

- 1996 was a record year for company mergers globally with companies worth $1.14 trillion joining up. This was 32 percent more than in 1995 which was the previous record year, according to U.S. research company Securities Data Corp.
- Six of ten Swedes would accept that Sweden's defence would become part of a common European defence programme.
- Some 500,000 new employees are needed by local governments for elderly-, child care and schools by the year 2005, but this does not mean the total number of workers will increase.

- In 10 years there might be only around 50 traditional post offices left in Sweden while more other outlets, such as stores, will offer postal services, general director Jan Freese says in an interview.

- Most big Swedish companies are expecting better results in 1997 than a year ago. A survey by Eureka Research of 100 of Sweden's 500 biggest companies found 52 percent were expecting higher profits this year, 33 percent unchanged and nine percent lower profits. A third of the companies expecting a profit lift had budgeted for an increase in profits of between 10 and 30 percent.
- The time for bargains in the market is past, according to mining group Trelleborg's managing director Kjell Nilsson in an interview. Now it is hard work that will pay off for companies.
- Finance Minister Erik Asbrink and the government are having trouble finding a new general director for Swedish National Economic Research Institute KI to replace Alf Carling.
